Title: Object-centred automated compliance checking: a novel, bottom-up approach
Authors: Omar Doukari; David Greenwood; Kay Rogage; Mohamad Kassem
Abstract: Building Information Modelling (BIM) is changing how built assets are delivered and operated. A built asset is represented as a set of objects, each with an identity, attributes, and relations. This object-oriented nature enables new approaches for ensuring compliance with a range of requirements (e.g. industry guidelines, project-specific requirements, building codes and standards). Furthermore, bottom-up design approaches are known to be more suitable for quality control and error detection. Based on an adapted simulated annealing concept, this paper proposes an automated compliance checking classification and identifies a set of desired characteristics that such methods should fulfill. It then demonstrates a bottom-up object-centered approach for automated model checking with a corresponding plugin prototype. The approach enables four key processes and satisfies all desired characteristics of compliance checking methods, including content validation, model completeness, smart object checking, and design option checking. Title: Multi-ontology fusion and rule development to facilitate automated code compliance checking using BIM and rule-based reasoning
Authors: Jiang Liu; Jianyong Shi; Chaoyu Wang
Abstract: This study presents a novel approach that combines multiple ontologies and rule-based reasoning to automate building code compliance checking using BIM. By fusing ontologies from different domains and formalizing compliance rules, the method enhances automated rule interpretation and reasoning in compliance checking. The approach uses BIM models (in IFC format) and a set of fused ontologies to represent regulatory knowledge, enabling an automated reasoning engine to check the BIM model against code requirements. Title: Automated code compliance checking through building information modelling
Abstract: The design, construction, and handover of building projects must comply with local authority rules. Manual assessment of drawings against complex rule sets is cumbersome, inconsistent, costly, and error-prone, causing major delays. This research develops an automated code compliance checking process using BIM. Shortcomings of manual code compliance were identified via a review of existing systems and confirmed through expert interviews. A new automated compliance checking system with BIM integration was then developed and evaluated. The automated BIM-based code checking process reduced review time from about one week to roughly six hours. However, feedback indicated that architects would require higher fees to produce complete BIM models. Title: Automated code compliance checking research based on BIM and knowledge graph
Abstract: Automated code compliance checking plays an important role in advancing the construction industry. While traditional drawing reviews rely on expert identification, this study aims to realize automatic code compliance review by using BIM technology combined with knowledge graph techniques. The proposed method uses a knowledge graph to transform textual code provisions into a computer-recognizable structured format via natural language processing, creating a human–machine-readable knowledge graph representation of the rules. For checking BIM models, the BIM data are exported and represented in RDF (using Protégé), and then mapping rules and review rules are applied to generate a compliance report. An example is presented to validate the feasibility of the approach. Title: Semantic web-based automated compliance checking with integration of Finite Element analysis
Authors: Panagiotis Patlakas; Ioannis P. Christovasilis; Lorenzo Riparbelli; Franco K. T. Cheung; Ermal Vakaj
Abstract: Automatic compliance checking (ACC) is a promising approach to ensure building designs meet regulations, especially using Building Information Modeling (BIM) and Industry Foundation Classes (IFC). However, engineering analyses like Finite Element Analysis (FEA) are often used by engineers and have seen little integration into ACC. This work proposes a holistic Semantic Web-based ACC framework that integrates FEA results into the IFC schema. A top-level Building Compliance Ontology (BCO) is introduced to encompass all aspects of regulatory compliance, with a novel focus on modeling regulatory statements (clauses) rather than just building components. To evaluate the approach, a real-world use case is tested: checking a modular steel structure’s design for compliance with structural code requirements. An open-source FEA solver is used and its results are embedded into the BIM/IFC model via an open-source middleware. The BCO is extended to cover structural engineering concepts, and appropriate ACC classes and SHACL rules are implemented. Compliance checking is then automatically performed by executing SHACL rules in a Semantic Web environment, successfully verifying the structure’s compliance with code provisions:contentReference[oaicite:13]{index=13}:contentReference[oaicite:14]{index=14}

Title: Automated Compliance Checking System for Structural Design Codes in a BIM Environment
Authors: Wonhui Goh; Jaeguk Jang; Sang I. Park; Bong-Hyuck Choi; Heuiseok Lim; Goangseup Zi
Abstract: This study proposes a framework for developing an automated compliance checking (ACC) system to verify structural design calculations in an openBIM (IFC) environment. The framework comprises four main components: (1) classifying design code provisions by structural component and limit state; (2) preparing a structural analysis model in accordance with the Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) schema; (3) interpreting the code requirements into a machine-readable rule format; and (4) designing the ACC system architecture, focusing on the flow of rule execution for structural code checks. The framework is demonstrated with a detailed example using ifcOWL, SWRL rules, and a Drools inference engine. A prototype ACC system was developed to check the strength and serviceability requirements of a prestressed concrete girder bridge. The system successfully verified an actual bridge design example. Title: Automated Building Information Modeling Compliance Check through a Large Language Model Combined with Deep Learning and Ontology
Authors: Nanjiang Chen; Xuhui Lin; Hai Jiang; Yi An
Abstract: Ensuring compliance with complex building standards and regulations during design is a significant challenge in the BIM domain. Manual compliance checking is inefficient and error-prone. Recent natural language processing (NLP) and deep learning methods have improved rule interpretation and checking, but they demand extensive feature engineering, large labeled datasets, and high computational resources. This study introduces an innovative automated compliance checking framework that integrates a large language model (LLM) with deep learning and ontology-based knowledge models. The LLM (with few-shot learning capability) is leveraged to reduce the need for large annotated datasets, while deep learning is used to preliminarily classify regulatory text sections, which improves the accuracy of structured information extraction by the LLM. By combining deep learning for text preprocessing with LLM-driven rule interpretation and an ontology for domain knowledge, the framework automates the processing of regulatory texts and significantly reduces manual intervention. Title: Automatic compliance checking of BIM models against quality standards based on ontology technology
Authors: Zhiliang Ma; Honggang Zhu; Xinglei Xiang; Žiga Turk; Robert Klinc
Abstract: This paper presents an ontology-based approach for automatically checking BIM models against established quality standards. Ontology technology is used to formalize the content of BIM quality standards, enabling computer-interpretable representations of the rules. An inference mechanism is then employed to assess a BIM model’s quality compliance with the given standard. A prototype implementation is developed to validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. Title: A Semantic Web and IFC-Based Framework for Automated BIM Compliance Checking
Authors: Lu Jia; Maokang Chen; Chen Chen; Yanfeng Jin
Abstract: Manual inspection of building design deliverables is time-consuming, labor-intensive, and prone to errors. With the development of BIM technology, automated rule compliance checking has become a trending solution. This paper presents a method that combines Semantic Web technologies with IFC-based data to enhance human–machine collaborative code compliance checking. First, a five-step process (integrated with domain specifications) is designed to construct a building object ontology that covers most architectural objects in the AEC domain. Next, a set of mapping rules is defined (based on how IFC entities express information) to create a semantic link between the ifcOWL representation of BIM data and the building object ontology. Then, by analyzing building regulations, generic SPARQL query templates are developed for major types of constraints. Title: BIM-Based Model Checking: A Scientometric Analysis and Critical Review
Authors: Sihao Li; Ziyang Jiang; Zhao Xu
Abstract: Building Information Modeling (BIM) has been widely applied throughout project lifecycles in the AEC industry, and errors in BIM models can lead to significant losses. This has driven increasing attention to BIM-based model checking (BMC) technologies. Despite numerous publications describing BMC methods, there has been a lack of systematic analysis and visualization of existing research. This paper conducts a combined scientometric analysis and critical review of BMC-related studies published from 2008 to 2024 in Web of Science and Scopus. The scientometric analysis objectively presents the state and evolution of the field using quantitative data (e.g. publication counts, author networks, citation analysis). The critical review then qualitatively examines the content of the literature, summarizing key research topics and current challenges. Finally, the study identifies promising future research directions for advancing BIM-based model checking.
